Rutile-TiO2 is a well-known wide band gap semiconductor, making it useful in various applications, yet it has inadequate light absorption capabilities in the visible spectrum. To address this limitation, a comprehensive theoretical investigation was undertaken using the spin-orbit coupling to examine the electronic and magnetic properties of rutile-TiO2 when carbon and nitrogen are substituted individually or in combination at Ti sites. Through careful analysis, concise explanations were provided for previously unexplained results found in experimental data. Notably, a substantial spontaneous magnetization of 2.55 uB was predicted along with a significantly enhanced light absorption capacity in the visible spectrum, when nitrogen was carefully displaced. These findings are highly significant and offer practical guidance for future experiments.

To top quark production in the Large Hadron Collider, the concept of "energy elasticity" is introduced as a novel approach to overcome existing constraints. Top quark production, particularly when the quark and antiquitter are at high momentum, is obscured by multijet backgrounds in the Large Hadron Collider. Introducing the notion of "elastic energy" - the kinetic energy of the quark and antiquark - is beneficial as it is simply conserved in the elastic production, unlike transverse momentum which has weaker constraints from quantum mechanics. The top quark and antiquark can remain in the same hadronic jet in the LHC, but this approach is advantageous as it is simply kinetic energy that's conserved in the top quark and antiquark. The proposed top quark production search relies solely on the two-body top quark and antiquark decay and claims top quark and/or "elastic energy" suppression raises top quark and/or "elastic energy" thresholds as little as 250 GeV on the LHC.

We build upon the concept of upper richness, a refinement of chromatic number introduced by Abrahamson and Seymour and Davisman, in the context of infinite graphs. Specifically, we introduce and explore the property of infinitely rich triangles in graphs, which can be viewed as a specialized variation of recently defined concepts including defectively chromatic triangles, insufficient triangles, and upper-rich triangles. Furthermore, we establish that every infinite graph without a critical path can be recolored using an infinite set of colors in such a way that all triangles formed by monochromatic edges are upper-rich, a result that generalizes a finding by Tu. Additionally, we discover that if a graph lacks both cycles of two specific colors, it is guaranteed to be upper infinitely rich. This latter concept, known as the infinite richness in Ramsey terms, was recently defined by Tu and we also prove that any graph with an infinite girth cannot be colored with a finite set of colors in such a way that it does not contain a monochromatic triangle. This last result mirrors a finding by de Joannis de Védris, which states that such graphs require an unbounded number of colors to avoid monochromatic triangles.

Our in-depth analysis of the quantum algorithms for scalar QED in $O (1) $-noise and $O (\log (n)) $-setting reveals that introducing qudit-based sQED simulations with $k$ levels yields superior outcomes compared to conventional qubit-based methods. This advantage holds particularly true in the high-mass regime, where it leads to more precise calculations of the vacuum energy density and magnetic susceptibility. These findings suggest that utilizing qudits can provide meaningful enhancements for future experimental applications.

In support of upcoming particle physics experiments, researchers have developed an efficient method to produce high-density polarized positrons. By using high-intensity laser pulses directed at a thin metallic layer, this method successfully generated dense streams of polarized positrons with a peak density of $10^{11} cm^{-3}$ and high polarization levels exceeding 90%. The process, predicted by strong physics theory, was experimentally verified and demonstrates the feasibility of producing high-quality positrons for future studies.

A polynomial basis factorization algorithm for a given permutation group has been developed by David, with the algorithm's efficiency directly linked to the "width" of the group. This relationship implies that groups exhibiting a specific property called "width" allow for an efficient solution to the conjugacy separation problem through the use of a modified Traverses' algorithm. Furthermore, we've established that certain classes of groups, including those built from specific simple groups like alternating and Lie groups of certain types, exhibit this property by dividing the number of conjugates of any element in the group.

This project develops a highly portable temperature sensor suitable for integrating into CMOS circuits. The sensor employs a subthreshold delay circuit to detect temperature changes, utilizing a positive feedback mechanism to minimize the reference current while maintaining high timing accuracy. The design includes two primary components: one generating a time delay that varies with temperature and another producing a comparable time delay for comparison. The device was put through rigorous testing on 55nm and 130nm processes, yielding highly accurate temperature readings. With a supply voltage range of 1.8V to 0.6V, the sensor offers 0.24°C resolution and begins conversion automatically upon voltage application. The total cost of converting temperature is $I_{bias} \times V_{DD} \times t_{conv} = 1.06nJ$ at the lowest supply setting of 0.6V with a conversion time of 100μs. The sensor covers a wide temperature range of -20°C to 120°C and was demonstrated to be highly accurate across this range.

This research focuses on developing various geometric structures, including connections, metrics, and bundles, within the context of Lie groupoids and differentiable stacks. We establish original results demonstrating that specific properties of these structures can imply the equivalent characteristics of underlying principal bundles. Notably, our findings provide new proofs of well-known theorems and offer novel approaches to previously proven concepts. Additionally, our methods facilitate the extension of prior works by enabling the generalization of certain constructions and interpretations, specifically relating the reduction of subgroups to invariant forms and metrics through the adoption of a new approach based on differential forms on manifolds.

Interstellar molecular clouds, where stars are born, contract through gravitational collapse and are shaped by the pressure of thermal and non-thermal gases. Although extensive research has been done on outer core regions, less is known about central dense clusters. Observations of a specific "dragon" infrared dark cloud reveal an expanding spherical structure at its center, with a speed of approximately 0.44 km/s. This discovery is particularly interesting because it contradicts standard theories of massive star formation, which rely on disk accretion, as no protostellar candidates have been found within this expanding region. Core expansion has been observed in other objects, but this is the first time such an phenomenon has been documented in a massive cluster precursor. We propose that the expansion is caused by the pressure of non-thermal gas, which can be produced by non-collisional processes such as Alfvn waves. The study of core dynamics is essential for comprehending the conditions necessary for massive star formation.

A Recurrence Relation is a mathematical equation that connects integer values of a parameter, often facilitating the efficient computation of large parameters from smaller ones. In applications involving image or video processing, where a parameter represents the number of pixels or time steps, a One-step Recurrence enables efficient computations across a fixed domain by linking adjacent time steps. Although Two-step Incidence Theorems are widely available for harmonic functions, they are of limited use in applications due to their dependence on boundary conditions rather than a fixed coefficient matrix. This study presents One-step Incidence Theorems for two types of stochastic fields representing random variations across a spherical surface, specifically for the Gegenbauer and Herglotz functions, thereby providing efficient algorithms for simulating these RSFs.
The friction coefficient of dry foams is influenced by their viscoelastic texture, following a root-friction power law that mirrors granular material behavior.

The rapid advancement of dermoscopy and imaging technology in recent years has significantly improved our ability to diagnose melanoma and other forms of skin cancer. However, the melasma that often plagues these images poses a significant obstacle to the reliable generalization of machine learning models across diverse patient populations. This melmasa interference underscores the critical nature of outlier detection in dataset sampling, presenting a pressing research challenge. To address this challenge, our proposed approach employs a lightweight version of the U-net architecture to extract detailed feature maps from dermoscopic images, which are then flattened and fed into a fully connected network to generate class predictions. To detect outlier samples, we developed a novel method that leverages the Toxer network, which utilizes two types of entropy measures - local and global - to identify samples that deviate from the norm. The study of a rotating Hele-Shaw cell containing a viscous fluid and subjected to radial pressure gradients sheds light on the effects of rotation rates and geometry on the interfacial behavior between the fluid and a less dense, inertial liquid. When the fluids are of comparable density, fingers of the inertial liquid extend into the viscous fluid beyond the onset of asymmetry. As the rotation increases or the cell's radius decreases, the interface becomes as wavy, the finger patterns become staggered in the radial direction, and eventually, the fingers close up and spiral, surpassing the point of asymmetry. In contrast, when the fluids have a substantial density difference and the fluid is more dense, fingers of the viscous fluid protrude into the inertial liquid. These fingers open up and overlap as the rotation rates increase or the cell's radius decreases, resulting in radial jets that shoot into the lighter liquid and form droplets at the outer edge of the cell. This study also examines the effects of radial curvature on the closure and reversal of lighter liquid fingers in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell.

Scientists have identified the spectra of two distinct isomers of cyclopentadiene, specifically ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its two forms alpha and beta, within the TMC-1 molecular cloud. This marks the initial detection of ethynyl cyclopentadiene in any astronomical setting. By comparing the relative quantities of different compounds within the TMP-1 molecular cloud, researchers have discovered that cyclical hydrocarbons exist primarily in forms containing cyanine, which may be applicable to other molecular settings as well. Furthermore, by studying the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers' relative quantities, a method has been developed to estimate the number of linear molecules within the TMC-1 environment. Additionally, an updated estimate for the total number of molecules within the TMC-1 environment has been produced based on literature data.

Neural machine translation (NMT) currently lacks effective generation guidance, a capability that enables knowledge transfer to models with limited knowledge and facilitates applications in key NMT challenges. We introduce look-ahead features essential for generating translations with NMT models, a novel framework based on partial words that comprises two methods: directly training a model to generate unworded fragments and leveraging strong teacher models to assess generation progress. We evaluate our approach through experiments on the NMT benchmark and find that: (1) assessing future generation potential significantly enhances alternative generation; (2) generating unworded fragments is successful with minimal sequence-to-sequence model modifications; and (3) simple unworded fragment models achieve substantial results, suggesting that future generation guidance can be effective even with limited model complexity.

The immense demand for computational power by big data, AI, and genomics posed significant challenges in 2011, prompting the U.S. National Academy of Sciences to call for a comprehensive assessment of high-performance computing. Rempe and Grobschedel, the authors, propose examining the evolution of large-scale computing from a different perspective — that of ordinary users. This article focuses on the development of grid computing, a movement driven by the desire to connect and utilize scattered computational resources, rather than the technology itself. From 1995 to 2005, grid computing saw rapid growth fueled by the anticipation of working with interconnected resources, leading to the integration of global computing power into large-scale systems. However, as highlighted by the failure of the DataGrid project, the path forward required departing from technology-centric approaches and embracing a more transformative perspective.

A non-equivalent unified dark matter model, where a class of non-equivalent matter particles makes up approximately 75% of the total dark sector, is studied under the framework of rheology with non-vanishing dissipative forces. In this model, the interplay between the gravitational interaction and a contact-type non-linear force, responsible for generating heat and friction, is analyzed to derive the Friedmann equations and the continuity equation for a dust fluid. By choosing specific contact force parameters, we are able to replicate the cosmic history observed in the $\Lambda$CDM model, while also accounting for the emergence of dark energy in the late universe. In order to calculate the parameters associated with dark matter and dark energy, we use H0 and S8 from the Planck data, as well as the cosmic age, and we obtain the following relationships: $\omega = \eta = 10^{-39}$ and $\rho_0^{dark\ matter} = 1.2 \cdot 10^{-29} g/cm^3$. In contrast, combining the H0, PANtheon and BAO parameters leads to the following results: $\rho_0^{dark\ matter} = 1.0 \cdot 10^{-29} g/cm^3$ and an equation of state parameter $w = -0.78$, which is in close agreement with previous findings.

Recent experimental findings indicating anomalies in $\gamma+$invisible decay channels of $J/\psi$ mesons may stem from the neutrino sector or a yet undiscovered particle, prompting thorough investigations into effective field theories. By deriving relationships between effective field theory coefficients and neutrino mass, previous results from SNO, Super-K, and other experiments which lack sensitivity to heavy neutrino contributions to effective field theory operators are also explored. This work introduces a novel multivariate functional singular cross-spectrum examination (MuRFSS) framework, building on an existing singular cross-spectrum analysis method. A significant breakthrough by Fu and Wang (2022) established that the local time $l_a(N)$ at point a, after N steps of a simple symmetric random walk, is bounded within $N$ steps for all points a, where N is sufficiently large compared to some power of $\log N$. This result was an improvement over the previous bond by Davis (1981). Building upon this foundation, we develop an arbitrary power bound $\epsilon$ for the ratio N/(\log N)^{1/3-\epsilon}, clarify and extend key lemmas from Fu and Wang's research, and utilize these refined findings to analyze the characteristics of the set of points where the local time remains bounded by N over N to 2N time periods. This enables us to determine the size and distribution of this set, its complement, and its connected components, thus proving that the ratio N/(\log N)^{1/3-\epsilon} has no upper bound.

The helicon mode of the IShTAR plasma source was characterized in terms of plasma potential, density, and temperature as functions of bias power and magnetic field strength.  A Langmuson probe collection current ratio method was used to derive floating potential first, and then plasma potential and voltage fluctuations were analyzed.  It was found that voltage fluctuations are related to sheath oscillations and that floating and plasma potentials are uncorrelated.  Next, it was shown that the collection current ratio method aligns with previous measurements of plasma density.  Finally, the relationship between the collection current ratio and the magnetic field was used to estimate the average plasma density along the source channel and validate the simulated density profiles from the PLASOP code.

The microscopic examination of tissue samples is a routine practice in pathology for disease diagnosis, and it heavily relies on a physician's ability to distinguish individual cells from their surrounding background. This task becomes increasingly difficult when cellular features blend into the tissue, obscuring key identifying characteristics of the cell. To address this challenge, researchers have developed a method that utilizes deep learning to isolate cell nuclei from their surroundings in digital images. Our proposed approach, which is based on a novel two-stage network, divides the problem into first segmenting normal cells and then focusing on abnormal cells. This method, in contrast to existing solutions, achieves more precise results with fewer parameters to process. Experimental results show that our model is 17% more efficient in terms of pixel segmentation and significantly improves cell detection accuracy.

We prove a local odd special isotropic exchange theorem for $O^{+}(2n+1,q)$ and $Sp_{2n}(q)$ for any $2$-power $n$ and prime $q$. This means that given two identical segments of length at least $\frac{10}{27}$ of $q$ in the characteristics of two isotropic forms which differ by an $\Gamma$ in both cases, any variation $\Gamma'$ can be applied to both forms to produce the same outcome, provided they are of the same type and size. This is part of a larger conjecture by Spivak and Tsfasman that applies to more complex, form that differ by $\Gamma$ within a certain distance of $q$.

We aim to provide a practical, mathematical explanation of how graph neural networks operate, focusing on the convolutional aspects of these algorithms. Our matched filtering perspective allows us to easily understand the fundamental operations of these complex systems. This approach enables us to derive the well-known GCN and KGCN methods from first principles. We contrast this straightforward interpretation with the difficult pseudospectral theory that underpins graph convolutions, making it clear how neural networks can efficiently process and navigate the intricacies of graph-based data.

In three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is shown to arise as a consistent sub-theory of a Chern-Simons (CS) action that includes a non-Abelian gauge field. By redefining the CS connection through the spacetime metric and gauge field via the Parke-Taylor map, we identify the equivalent first-order Hilbert-Palatini action paired with the gauge field's CS term. This reformulation allows us to seamlessly switch between the two formulations. Using this approach, we analyze a rotating black hole solution within the extended phase space. The rotation parameter of this black hole varies based on the gauge field's flux, with specific flux values. At certain flux values typical of solitons, the black hole's horizon vanishes, converting the solution into a boson star soliton. This relationship holds true regardless of the gauge field's non-Abelian nature. As a result, with appropriate flux values, the metric of this solution becomes indistinguishable from that of a previously reported pure gravity solution, albeit with differing critical exponents in the van der Waals-like behavior. This outcome is accompanied by another solution featuring time-dependent metrics and gauge fields.

Elastography, an ultrasound-based imaging method, improves the detection of cancer by visualizing the varying stiffness of tissues. However, images distorted by curved interfaces due to the lateral displacement of tissue strands, also known as shear ballastment effect, remain a significant challenge. Although previous research attempted to mitigate this issue, previous methods relied on inaccurate estimations of the effective displacement estimation because of the impossibility of directly measuring the source shear wave in clinical settings. In order to address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that accurately estimates the effective source of a linear array scanner, and subsequently employs a synthetic aperture reconstruction to produce clear images free from distortion. In order to evaluate the efficacy of this technique, we conducted a thorough assessment of the results of this technique that surpassed previous methods that led to distorted images or failed when encountering interfaces.

Imperative algorithms, which describe desired outcomes without necessarily explaining how to achieve them, are commonly used to present computing methods. However, verifying that an algorithm produces correct results can be challenging. This work introduces an alternative presentation format - logical pseudocode, which adapts formal proof techniques, specifically invariant-based reasoning, into a practical guide. This approach uses intuitive concepts such as preconditions, assertions, and postconditions to represent algorithms, establishing a connection between computing methods and verifying their reliability. This abstract discusses the benefits of using logical pseudocode and demonstrates its application with simple examples, including fundamental data structure operations like list insertions and searches.

In the context of dynamic data streams, we propose a randomized algorithm for the k-centers clustering problem that ensures the size of an approximate solution remains within a factor of $O(\sqrt{k})$ of the optimal solution, with high confidence, as the algorithm processes updates to the dataset in real-time. This factor of $O(\sqrt{k})$ can be reduced to $2.236k$ or $2\cdot k$ under specific conditions on the number of data points. Our solution utilizes $O(k^2 d \cdot \text{polylog}(n))$ memory, where n represents the total number of points, k is the desired number of centers, and d denotes the number of dimensions. For scenarios where the number of dimensions is significantly larger than the square of the number of desired centers, our solution requires only $O(k \cdot \text{polylog}(n))$ memory. Notably, our approach builds on a breakthrough result by Andoni et al. (SODA 2019), which achieved a constant approximation factor for dynamic k-centers clustering in terms of dimensions but with very large constant values.

We introduce a novel hierarchical approach to resolving complex, multi-agent, stochastic, finite-horizon, non-zero-sum, chase-evasion games through the breakdown of their planning horizons into smaller, manageable subgames for adaptive strategy adjustment by agents. To boost the precision of standard model predictions for future high-energy muon colliders, a improved version of the vector boson approximation (VBA) has been developed. The E-VBA standardizes the calculation of 2-to-4 particle processes by reorganizing the amplitude in the t and u channels, allowing individual helicity amplitudes to represent particle production after radiating a vector boson. In contrast to the original VBA, the E-VBA enables a more precise calculation of phase-space suppression at lower energies and reduced final-state radiation effects when using narrow-width and parton shower approximations in Monte Carlo generators. This tool is available as a Python module that can be integrated with existing tools like MadGraph5_aMC@NLO for comprehensive analysis.

This article historical narrative centers on four individuals: Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. It details how Godel discovered a flaw in a proof for the completeness of first-order logic, a theorem originally proved by Church and later by Turing. When Turing passed away, Tarski stepped in to collaborate with them. Building on the work of Kosei and Muschik, we extend the B-conjecture for functions, specifically for functions within the Specker-Arvesse class, which encompasses all entire functions whose Taylor series' coefficients decrease at a rate of O(n^B). A key property of these functions is the three balls formula, where the value of a function within an intermediate sphere can be bounded by the geometric mean of the maximum values of the function within two larger spheres. For functions in this class, we prove a similar relationship holds for functions u in the real monogenic polynomials, such that the maximum value of u within a smaller sphere is bounded by the geometric mean of the maximum values of u within two larger spheres. This result is achieved by leveraging the properties of the Dirac operator and the use of Cayley transforms to establish a connection between the radii of the spheres in question.

We formulate inverse problem solutions as the generation of a conditional probability distribution and investigate the use of conditional generative adversarial networks (CGANs) for this purpose, which we term Inverse- CGANs.  To achieve a feasible solution, we apply a score normalization technique to transform an unsolved uniform sampling problem into the post-estimation of a conditional probability in the inverse problem.  Experimental results on compressed sensing MRI and MRI k-space completion demonstrate the Inverse-CGAN's ability to produce high-quality reconstructions with identified probability distributions that are closely matched to ground truth.  In contrast to existing methods, our approach directly learns (1) a complex, non-Gaussian mapping between data and latent variables, and 2) an associated conditional probability in an adversarial setting.

The scintillation pattern of the pulsar B1133+16 has been meticulously analyzed using six and a half years of data from the NANOGrav 12-month dataset, which allowed researchers to identify a significant amount of regular scintillation produced by the interstellar medium near the Earth-pulsar path. By simming the scintillation patterns, scientists have been able to map out the three-dimensional distribution of interstellar gas around our galaxy and discover that a vast cavity extends from the center, spanning a radius exceeding 25 kiloparsecs. This discovery has been further broken down into a middle layer where the pulsar resides and causes the observed scintillation effects, and it is hypothesized that a scintillating shell may exist above this layer. A statistical study of multiple pulsars indicates that smaller voids may exist on both sides of the galaxy.

This paper presents a significant improvement on WaveNet models for the natural synthesis of speech and musical sounds. We propose a novel architecture called the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, which combines the flexibility of autoregressive generative models with a novel use of dilated convolution neural networks. We achieve this by tailoring the network's depth to the pitch of a sound, allowing sounds with both transient and periodic components to be modelled effectively within the same framework. The proposed model has demonstrated superior performance, outperforming previous deep generative models and even a simple Nearest Neighbor baseline, with minimal training time, for speech and sound generation tasks.

This article formally establishes key outcomes related to the concept of shadow bicategories in category theory. Cross-domain image generation models, such as GANS, demonstrate success in creating images across different realms, but a key issue is that these outputs often lack a connection to the original, "real" images in their respective domains. In contrast, in applied fields like medicine, it's crucial for synthesized anomalies to be distinctly separated from actual images and other artificial defects to effectively support anomaly detection training. While feasible, this challenge is complicated to accomplish due to the difficulty of creating synthetic images with distinct "noise" images to other artificial defects to effectively support anomaly detection training. This paper introduces a novel, two-step approach: first, real images are made inconclusive by mixing them with the target domain and adding Gaussian noise, and then the noisy images are used to generate a distinct visual output using a style transfer algorithm. This method was successfully applied to create synthetic anomalies for CT scans and MRI images of normal brains, achieving improved classification accuracy and anomaly detection performance.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
Tsallis delay, a variation of the power law, and investigate its implications.
Our analysis reveals that this model allows for delayed choices and demonstrates

We further apply our model to actual data, comparing it with traditional log-linear

A key distinction between standard General Relativity and Hefty Gravity lies in the validity of the harmonic gauge when applied to the linearized field equations.  In General Relativity, choosing the harmonic gauge simplifies these equations significantly, turning them into the well-known wave equation with a source term representing stress-energy.  However, in the case of Hefty Gravity with its cubic non-linearity, the harmonic gauge provides no such simplification.  Despite this limitation, the harmonic gauge's name originates from its transformation into the wave equation in linearized gravity, a property that remains applicable to Hefty Gravity as well.  This characteristic gives the harmonic gauge practical value in solving initial value problems within this framework.  Furthermore, the harmonic gauge's utility is evident when comparing the solutions of Hefty Gravity and GR, both of which satisfy the same harmonic gauge conditions and initial data, yet yield different results due to their distinct non-linear expansions.

Quantum mechanics is effectively illustrated by Weyl quantization, a framework where a Weyl symbol $f \in \mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{2d})$ defines a corresponding quantum operator. Despite its advantages, Weyl quantization presents challenges when establishing the quantum-to-classical transition, as it fails to preserve the commutative property of classical phase space functions' composition. This short paper explores the representation of canonical equilibrium states within the Weyl-Wigner framework, offering a basic analysis of this approach.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been supported by numerous recent studies and thoughts. Our analysis builds on the work of multiple groups, including those led by S. G. Johnson, J. C. Vilela Do Amaral, L. Tsunoda, and the ANR project TEMPS, as well as our own findings. We annotate and discuss the results, deriving new relationships between them. Our main discovery is that a certain condition, first introduced by Ramsey in 1956, can be fulfilled, indicating that negative temperatures can exist in the electronic spin systems of molecules, specifically in benzene, naphthalene, and anthracene. This contrasts with earlier theories that used solid-state spin chains as models, which have been shown to contain infinite numbers of particles and excitations, are boundless, and interact with each other through infinitely strong forces. Consequently, these models lead to the conclusion that negative temperatures always arise, but in unrealistic ways. However, our research demonstrates that, despite being composed of only 14 carbon atoms each, benzene, naphthalene, and anthracene exhibit the capacity to reach the "regime" of negative temperatures while remaining fully in line with Einstein's special theory of relativity. We argue that this implies the concept of negative absolute temperature is not as contradictory or nonsensical as it has been widely regarded to be.

Within the simplest "scoto-seesaw" frameworks, we examine the conditions that ensure the electroweak scale remains stable, alongside the implications for an additional neutral dark matter particle found among the model's extra singlet states. In the traditional versions of these theories, we find the scale of new physics must not surpass $10^{14}$ GeV, with the minimum allowed dark matter component accounting for roughly 10 percent of its total abundance. A later analysis of these "scoto-seesaw" models reveals a significant constraint: they struggle to explain the small mass of the observed dark matter particle. Nevertheless, a revised model can account approximately 128 orders of magnitude for the dark matter mass while avoiding the issues found in its later stages. This revised model also predicts the scale of new physics must not exceed $10^{11}$ GeV, with the smallest dark matter abundance being around $10^{-7}$ times the scale of new physics squared.

In this paper, we employ both regular and rotated crystal field coordinate systems to analyze and clarify the blurring of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital distinctiveness when considering transition metal oxides with a cubic environment, particularly those containing 4d, 5d, and p subshells. By utilizing a straightforward model, we demonstrate how the interaction between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals in these materials results in six unique combinations of bonded states, rather than maintaining separate $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ categories. We use an intuitive notation to describe these states, supported by visual representations in rotated crystal field coordinates. Our findings highlight the inappropriate use of traditional $t_{2g}$/$e_g$ nomenclature in various phenomena observed in 4d, 5d, and p block transition metal oxines, such as double exchange, magnetoelectric effects, and multiferroic behaviors.

We have developed a standalone birational invariant in symplectic geometry that extends the concepts of Betti numbers and Chern classes. This new invariant, called the relative Chern class, forms a homomorphism from the relative Chern ring to the cohomology ring. In particular, it maps elements of the relative Chern ring to actual cohomology classes rather than formal power series. The innovative approach involves integrating Geisser's definition of the Chern ring over the appropriate variable. Like their classical counterparts, relative Chern classes adhere to standard properties including compatibility with standard symplectic geometry, invariance under symplectic transformations, and additivity under certain symplectic transformations that glue manifolds. Most notably, we prove that just as their classical counterparts, relative Chern classes also behave flexibly under birational transformations that blow-up and blow-down.

This paper explores the concept of being able to deliberately depict specific medical conditions in patient imaging when the underlying anatomy is normal.  Knowing this can significantly enhance methods that improve diagnostic accuracy from imaging by allowing practitioners to compare actual imaging with altered versions depicting the illness.  To put this capability in practice, our research develops a framework consisting of two parts: first, a method to change imaging to reflect an absence of a disease, and second, a way to intentionally introduce a specific medical condition.  We propose evaluating this framework's effectiveness on the accurate depiction of illnesses, particularly in imaging related to pneumonia.
